{
  "frontend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement frontend handling so that any HTTP 404 response from single-item GET, PUT, or DELETE requests is treated as "item not found" and never reveals or displays another user's resource. Requirements and steps:

1) Contract with backend (must be implemented exactly as specified by backend team):
   - For single-item GET, PUT, DELETE endpoints, when the current requester is a non-owner ordinary user and the item exists, the backend will return HTTP 404 with a JSON body: {"detail": "Item not found"}.
   - For requests for a non-existing item, the backend will also return the same HTTP 404 and JSON body.
   - Owners and superusers retain their existing behaviors (successful responses, 403 where previously appropriate, etc.).
   - List endpoints are unchanged and continue to return only items the current user is allowed to see.

2) Error handling changes to implement in the frontend:
   - For single-item GET/PUT/DELETE responses, treat any response with HTTP status 404 and a JSON body containing detail == "Item not found" as a not-found condition. Do not display any item fields or partial data in this case.
   - Do not display a different message for an existing-but-forbidden item vs a genuinely non-existent item. Both must be handled identically (e.g., show a standard "Item not found" UI state/modal/snackbar/message).
   - Ensure UI does not leak or cache other users' data when receiving this 404. Specifically:
     - Do not populate detail views, edit forms, or confirmation dialogs with data from a failed fetch that returned 404.
     - If the UI previously cached an item from another user, clear or invalidate that cache on receiving the 404 for that item ID before rendering.
   - For PUT/DELETE flows: if the server returns the 404 described above, abort the operation, do not show success or partial-success UI, and display the standard "Item not found" error state.

3) UX guidance (minimal, consistent behavior):
   - The presentation for this 404 should be identical to the presentation for a not-found item that truly does not exist (e.g., redirect to a list view with a toast "Item not found", or show an in-place not-found message). The product team decides exact wording/placement; the frontend must use the backend message content only for internal logic (match exact string "Item not found"), and display a localized/text-wrapped version per UI guidelines.

4) Implementation details and checks:
   - Detect status code == 404 and JSON body.detail === "Item not found". Do not rely on status text, headers, or proprietary fields.
   - Do not special-case based on any 403 or other codes for this behavior — only the 404+detail combo is guaranteed by the backend contract.
   - Ensure retry logic or optimistic UI updates do not reveal resource fields after receiving this 404. Cancel any pending re-fetches for that item ID until the user navigates away or explicitly attempts a different operation.

5) Tests to add or update (automated and manual acceptance tests):
   - Automated: simulate backend returning 404 with {"detail":"Item not found"} for GET/PUT/DELETE on an item owned by another user; assert the UI shows the not-found state and no item fields are rendered.
   - Automated: simulate backend returning 404 for an actually non-existent item; assert identical UI behavior to the previous test.
   - Automated: simulate backend success for owner and superuser; assert normal behavior unchanged.
   - Manual: verify cached item scenarios do not display another user's data after receiving the 404.

6) Non-goals / preserved behaviors:
   - Do not change list endpoints or their rendering logic; lists must continue to show only items the current user can see.
   - Do not change backend authentication/authorization flows—frontend only reacts to the specified 404 contract.

Notes for implementers: do not assume endpoint URL patterns or authentication mechanisms; wire this behavior into your existing fetch/HTTP client layer so it applies uniformly for single-item GET/PUT/DELETE across the app."
  },
  "backend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement backend behavior to ensure ordinary (non-owner, non-superuser) users receive HTTP 404 with JSON body {"detail": "Item not found"} when they attempt GET, PUT, or DELETE on another user's existing item. This response must be identical to the response for a genuinely non-existent item. Owners and superusers keep their existing permissions; list endpoints remain unchanged. Requirements and steps:

1) Contract to expose to frontend (must be implemented exactly):
   - For single-item GET, PUT, DELETE endpoints, when the requesting user is NOT the owner of the item and NOT a superuser, return HTTP 404 with response body (JSON): {"detail": "Item not found"}.
   - When the requested item ID does not exist, return the same HTTP 404 and JSON body.
   - Do not return 403 or any other distinguishing status or message in these non-owner cases; the client must not be able to distinguish existence vs ownership based on status or message.
   - Owners and superusers retain full existing behavior (success responses or existing error semantics for invalid input, etc.).
   - List endpoints must continue to enumerate only items visible to the current user (no change required).

2) Implementation guidance (framework-agnostic):
   - Fetch the item by ID internally (database query) as usual.
   - If item is not found: return HTTP 404 with JSON {"detail": "Item not found"}.
   - If item is found:
       a) If current user is owner OR current user is superuser: proceed with normal endpoint logic (return item for GET, apply update for PUT, perform delete for DELETE).
       b) If current user is neither owner nor superuser: do NOT return 403 or expose item data. Instead immediately return HTTP 404 with JSON {"detail": "Item not found"}.
   - Ensure no item fields or metadata are included in the 404 response and no headers leak owner-specific info.

3) Error responses and consistency:
   - Use Content-Type: application/json and the exact JSON body key and value: {"detail": "Item not found"}.
   - Do not vary the body or status for this ownership-based hiding behavior.
   - Preserve existing behavior for other error cases and status codes where applicable (validation errors for owners, auth failures for unauthenticated requests, etc.). If existing behavior for unauthenticated requests is different, do not change it unless the product explicitly instructs so.

4) Logging and auditing:
   - You may log authorization failures for internal audit, but do not include item-sensitive data in logs that could be displayed to the requester. Keep audit logs internal only.

5) Tests to add or update (automated and manual acceptance tests):
   - Automated unit/integration tests that assert:
       • Owner GET returns 200 and item payload unchanged.
       • Superuser GET returns 200 and item payload unchanged.
       • Non-owner GET for an existing item returns 404 with {"detail": "Item not found"} and no item payload.
       • Non-owner GET for a non-existent item returns 404 with {"detail": "Item not found"} (identical to previous case).
       • Repeat same set for PUT and DELETE: owner/superuser allowed; non-owner receives 404 with exact JSON body.
       • List endpoint tests unchanged—list returns only visible items for the current user.
   - Manual acceptance: verify frontend integration: a normal user attempting to GET/PUT/DELETE another user's existing item receives 404+detail and the frontend does not display item details.

6) Backward-compatibility and rollout notes:
   - This change intentionally collapses "forbidden/existing" and "not found" semantics into a single 404 response for non-owners. Do not alter other endpoints or user roles beyond this scope.
   - Communicate the exact error body and HTTP status to frontend implementers so they can match on status == 404 and body.detail == "Item not found".

7) Non-goals / constraints:
   - Do not change list endpoint visibility rules.
   - Do not assume or require any specific authentication mechanism; use the current auth context to determine current user and whether they are a superuser.

Important: Do not invent additional response fields or alternative error messages; the frontend is expected to match the literal JSON {"detail": "Item not found"} on HTTP 404 for these cases."
  }
}
